title: The Grapple with the Fever-Demon
story:
Vana, the thousand-armed demon king, had met Krishna and his kinsmen in battle outside his city of Sonitpura, and to help Vana the god Shiva had sent creatures of his own to fight — among them Jvara, the demon of fever. Jvara's burning weapon had very nearly consumed Balarama, Krishna's elder brother, before Krishna put the fire out with an embrace. Now the field lay empty around the two of them, and Krishna had called the demon out. "Come and fight with me," he had said. "Show me the full extent of your strength and power in this battle."

Jvara — three-legged, three-headed, six-armed, nine-faced, and never without his consuming weapon — answered with the weapon already burning. Around them the field had emptied: the demon army had fled, and only the two of them stood face to face in the middle of it.

With his right hand Jvara hurled his great burning weapon straight at Krishna's body. It struck home, and for a few moments Krishna felt it burning. Then the fire went out. It had touched him, spent itself against him, and died — the way fire dies when it meets what it cannot consume.

Then Jvara came at him, his long arms reaching like serpents. He struck Krishna on the neck and dealt him a blow across the breast, and there in the middle of the field a great duel began between the fever-demon and the man who would not be moved. The sound of their blows rolled across the plain like thunder against a mountain summit. Blow for blow they traded strokes that would have felled whole armies. The demon could range through the sky; Krishna stood planted on his ground. And strange to hear above the din, words kept coming out of the fight as if one fighter were teaching the other: "Do not strike this way. Strike this way."

For a long moment Krishna — who in truth was the lord of the universe, hidden in the body of a man — fought as if his own end were possible, as if this one body were all he had. Then he caught the fever-demon in his arms and began to crush him, grinding the golden, sky-ranging Jvara the way a pestle grinds grain, until the demon's strength ran out of him like water from a broken jar. The whole duel had lasted a moment. That moment decided everything.

At last Krishna threw the broken Jvara down upon the earth, and for a moment he believed the field was won.

But the fever-demon, released from that crushing embrace, did not flee the field. He did what no beaten enemy had done before: he entered Krishna's body and was gone.
reflection: In the midst of the duel come strange words of instruction, 'Do not strike this way, strike this way,' as though the fight itself were a lesson being given and received. And Krishna, wearing a mortal body, lets the burning touch him for a few moments before it goes out: even what wounds him is held within his own order.
content_note: A wrestling duel between Krishna and the demon Jvara; described without gore.
